appraisal_events.evidence: « Chaque fois je lui écrivis de n'en rien faire, en invoquant l'excuse d'être obligé de m'absenter [...] pour aller remplir [...] un devoir de famille avec ma grand'mère » ; « l'amitié n'est pas seulement dénuée de vertu comme la conversation, elle est de plus funeste » ; « je me mentais à moi-même [...] quand je me félicitais d'être aimé, admiré, par un être aussi bon, aussi intelligent, aussi recherché que Saint-Loup ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator repeatedly turns away Saint-Loup's offered visits under a fabricated family pretext in order to keep the afternoons with the little band, and then backs the refusal with a sustained argument that friendship is a worthless and even harmful abdication of self. Saint-Loup is thereby excluded from the narrator's valued space and his affection and admiration are recast as something to be repudiated rather than prized.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Ce n'était pas seulement une matinée mondaine, une promenade avec Mme de Villeparisis que j'eusse sacrifiées au "furet" ou aux "devinettes" de mes amies » ; « C'est avec délices que j'écoutais leur pépiement » ; les voix des jeunes filles ont « plus de notes que le plus riche instrument », jouées avec « l'ardeur des petits anges musiciens de Bellini ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Albertine and the other girls of the little band are preferred, explicitly and comparatively, to society (Mme de Villeparisis) and to friendship (Saint-Loup), and the narrator lavishes admiring perception on their faces and voices as inexhaustibly individual. The pleasure taken among them is endorsed as at least free of the lie the narrator imputes to friendship.

status_effects.explanation: He is kept out of the valued space of the passage: his proposed visits to Balbec are refused several times with a false excuse, and he is left to learn from his aunt what the alleged family duty really was.
His affection has no purchase here: he seeks the meeting, the narrator evades it, and the narrator treats his own gratification at being loved and admired by Saint-Loup as self-deception.
She is locally raised by being chosen over both worldly engagements and friendship, and by the narrator's delighted attention to her authority of tone and the singularity of her voice.

As one of the girls preferred to Saint-Loup and Mme de Villeparisis, she shares the passage's admiring individuation, her grave manner and Périgord-inflected voice being read as a distinctive personal signature.

He holds the floor with a long, forceful argument that subordinates friendship and conversation to solitary inward growth, and claims a connoisseur's discernment of voices, speaking from a position of judgment rather than being judged.

ambiguities: Saint-Loup is praised in the same sentence that demotes him — « un être aussi bon, aussi intelligent, aussi recherché » — so the negative movement plausibly attaches only to his relational claim on the narrator, not to his personal worth; the passage also concedes « Sans doute me jugea-t-il mal » and hedges the justification with « je n'avais peut-être pas tort », which weakens but does not cancel the narrator's endorsement of the refusal.

The elevation of the girls is qualified by late irony: their talk is called « peu intéressantes », their expressions are borrowed from parents (« Je trouverais cela assez terrible » ; « Ah ! c'est bien, sa peinture ? »), and they are described as ductile matter. A reading in which Albertine and Andrée are elevated only as aesthetic spectacle, and mildly diminished as persons, is defensible; the admiring, preference-establishing movement is taken here as dominant.
